lessons.title: Build an equation or formula
lessons.summary: Turn a relationship into symbols, use the equality and explain what the answer counts.
lessons.objective: Turn a relationship into symbols, use the equality and explain what the answer counts.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Name the unknown, write the two amounts, then put an equals sign between them.

Write the result with the units or a word that tells what the number counts.

Write a formula that works for every allowed value of the input.
lessons.method:
When should I write an equals sign?

An expression describes an amount. An equation says two amounts have the same value. Find the two amounts in the story.

How can an equation find a count?

Use one letter for the unknown count and write down what each term measures. Then use inverse operations to isolate the count.

How can I write a rule for changing totals?

Use letters for both the input and the total. Work out which terms repeat for each new group.
mistakes: Give the fixed charge its own term if it is paid once.
Check the answer in the original situation, including its units.
A fixed part is counted once, however many groups there are.

examples.title: Write an equation for the total cost
examples.question: A craft class charges £6 to join and £4 for each session. Tari pays £26 for \(x\) sessions. Write an equation in \(x\).
examples.solution:
The session charge is \(4x\). Add the joining charge once.

The cost \(6+4x\) must equal \(26\).

The answer is \(6+4x=26\).

examples.title: Use the equation to find a count
examples.question: A robot already has 7 recorded trips. It records 5 more trips each hour until it has 37. After how many hours does it reach that total?
examples.solution:
Let \(x\) be the number of hours. The total gives \(7+5x=37\).

Subtract 7 and divide by 5.

The answer is \(6\).

examples.title: Write a formula with a fixed and a changing part
examples.question: A rowing club puts 8 rowers in every boat. It also has 8 coaches. Write a formula for the total number \(t\) of people when it uses \(n\) boats.
examples.solution:
The boats hold \(8n\) rowers altogether.

Add \(8\) coaches to that count.

The answer is \(t=8n+8\).

lessons.title: Solving linear equations
lessons.summary: Keep both sides equal when solving for x with brackets or unknown terms on both sides.
lessons.objective: Keep both sides equal when solving for x with brackets or unknown terms on both sides.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Apply each inverse operation to both sides.

Combine the x terms on one side and the constants on the other.

When isolating an intact bracket, remove the outside operations before changing what is inside.
lessons.method:
Which operation should I undo first?

Solve by leaving the x term alone, then finding the value of one x.

What if x is on both sides?

Remove the smaller x term from each side to keep one positive coefficient. You can also solve with a negative coefficient if you keep its sign.

What if x is inside a bracket?

You can treat an intact bracket as a single quantity, or expand it carefully. Look for an inverse operation that keeps the steps short.
mistakes: Subtracting on the left requires subtracting the same amount on the right.
The sign changes only because you have added or subtracted a term on both sides.
When expanding instead, multiply every term inside the bracket.

examples.title: Solve a linear equation
examples.question: Solve \(5x+6=31\).
examples.solution:
Subtract \(6\) from both sides, so \(5x=25\).

Divide both sides by \(5\).

The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: Solve a linear equation
examples.question: Solve \(11x+7=5x+43\).
examples.solution:
Subtract \(5x\) from both sides. This leaves \(6x+7=43\).

Subtract 7 and divide by 6.

The answer is \(6\).

examples.title: Solve a linear equation
examples.question: Solve \(7(x+6)-8=83\).
examples.solution:
Add \(8\) to each side to leave \(7(x+6)=91\).

Divide both sides by 7. Then take 6 away from each side.

The answer is \(7\).

lessons.title: Changing the subject of a simple formula
lessons.summary: Make one letter the subject using inverse operations where the subject appears once.
lessons.objective: Make one letter the subject using inverse operations where the subject appears once.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Undo the last operation used on the new subject, then undo earlier operations.

When an entire expression is divided, multiply the entire other side by the denominator.

Read the output as a rule in the remaining letter.
lessons.method:
What does the subject mean?

The subject is the letter isolated on one side. Changing the subject expresses the same relationship in a different order.

How can I remove a denominator?

Multiply both sides by the denominator. Then continue to undo operations until the intended letter is alone.

How can I check the new rule?

Choose simple numbers to check one example in both versions. The formula should reproduce the same relationship.
mistakes: Keep the terms grouped with a bracket or a fraction bar.
A division by a constant can be undone by multiplying by that constant.
A quick numerical check can reveal a sign error. Keep the rearrangement as your mathematical justification.

examples.title: Make x the subject
examples.question: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=5x+4\).
examples.solution:
Subtract \(4\) from both sides, giving \(p-4=5x\).

Divide both sides by \(5\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{p-4}{5}\).

examples.title: Make x the subject
examples.question: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=\frac{6x}{5}\).
examples.solution:
Multiply both sides by \(5\) to remove the denominator.

Divide both sides by \(6\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{5p}{6}\).

examples.title: Rearrange and use a simple formula
examples.question: The value of \(q\) is given by \(q=8+6a\). Write a formula giving \(a\) in terms of \(q\).
examples.solution:
Subtract \(8\) from each side before dividing.

Divide the resulting expression by \(6\).

The answer is \(a=\frac{q-8}{6}\).

lessons.title: Simultaneous linear equations
lessons.summary: Find an ordered pair by elimination or substitution, then check it in both equations.
lessons.objective: Find an ordered pair by elimination or substitution, then check it in both equations.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Add for opposite coefficients. Subtract for equal coefficients.

Use the whole expression when replacing it. Solve the remaining equation in one letter.

Arrange like terms in the same columns so you can see what cancels.
lessons.method:
Which terms can I cancel?

An ordered pair must satisfy both equations. Adding two equalities can remove a letter when its coefficients are opposites.

When is substitution shorter?

If a letter is already alone, replace that letter in the other equation with its expression.

How can I form two equations from the facts?

Define both unknowns with a unit. Each total gives a separate equation in the same two unknowns.
mistakes: After finding one letter, substitute it to find the other.
Put the two values back in the same order as the requested pair.
Use asked price order when you give the final pair.

examples.title: Find a pair that fits both equations
examples.question: Solve the simultaneous equations \(5x+y=25\) and \(4x-y=11\). Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
examples.solution:
Add the two equations to remove y. The equal and opposite coefficients cancel.

The result is \(9x=36\). Solve for x, then use the first equation to find y.

The answer is \((4,5)\).

examples.title: Find a pair that fits both equations
examples.question: Solve \(y=6x-24\) and \(5x+y=31\) together. Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
examples.solution:
Use the expression for \(y\) from the first equation in the second equation.

Collect the terms to get \(11x=55\). After dividing, substitute to find \(y\).

The answer is \((5,6)\).

examples.title: Find a pair that fits both equations
examples.question: A receipt shows 13 large craft packs and one small pack cost £85. Another shows 6 large packs and one small pack cost £43. Find both prices. Give (large, small) in pounds.
examples.solution:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the larger and smaller pack prices, in pounds. The two receipts give \(13x+y=85\) and \(6x+y=43\).

Subtract the second equation from the first. This leaves \(7x=42\). Use the first receipt to find the small pack price.

The answer is \((6,7)\).

lessons.title: Solving equations with fractions (Extended)
lessons.summary: Clear numeric or linear denominators and check candidates against the original equation.
lessons.objective: Clear numeric or linear denominators and check candidates against the original equation.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Clear numerical denominators using a common multiple.

State the restriction, multiply through, then reject any excluded candidate.

Check the answer in the original equation with both denominators.

Multiply each term on both sides by the same product, then check the candidates against the original restrictions.
lessons.method:
How do I clear a numerical denominator?

Multiply both sides by a common denominator. If either side has several terms, multiply all of them.

What if a denominator contains the unknown?

Before clearing the denominator, decide which x would make it zero. That value is outside the original equation.

What if there are fractions on both sides?

Record both restrictions and multiply by both denominators. Cross-multiplication gives the same cleared equation in this layout.

How do I combine several fractions in an equation?

Choose a product of denominators so every fraction can be cleared in one line. Simplify the result and solve the new equation.
mistakes: A fraction bar groups all the terms in the numerator.
A simplified equation may be defined at a value where the original one is undefined.
A cross-product method applies to an equality between fractions.
Include a term with no fraction when multiplying through.

examples.title: Clear denominators to solve an equation
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{4x+24}{4}=11\).
examples.solution:
Multiply both sides by \(4\) to clear the denominator.

Subtract \(24\) and divide by \(4\).

The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: Clear denominators to solve an equation
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{55}{x+5}=5\).
examples.solution:
First record \(x\ne -5\), so the denominator can be multiplied through.

Multiply both sides by \(x+5\). Subtract \(25\) from both sides and divide by \(5\).

The answer is \(6\).

examples.title: Clear denominators to solve an equation
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{x+8}{x+6}=\frac{15}{13}\).
examples.solution:
Exclude \(x\ne -6\). Multiply both denominators through to cross-multiply.

Collect terms: \(-2x=-14\). Divide by \(-2\) and check the original denominator.

The answer is \(7\).

examples.title: Clear two algebraic denominators
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{128}{x-1}-\frac{126}{x+1}=1\). Give all roots.
examples.solution:
Exclude \(x=\pm1\). Multiply every term by \((x-1)(x+1)\).

Expand and rearrange to \(x^2-2x-255=0\). Factorise as \((x-17)(x+15)=0\); neither candidate was excluded.

The answer is \(x=-15\ \text{or}\ x=17\).

lessons.title: Solving quadratic equations (Extended)
lessons.summary: Choose factorisation, a completed square or the quadratic formula to find all real roots.
lessons.objective: Choose factorisation, a completed square or the quadratic formula to find all real roots.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Find both root values, then check them against the original equation.

If the constant is positive, take both signs before solving the two linear equations.

Use the signed coefficients in the quadratic formula and put the whole numerator above 2a.
lessons.method:
When can I use two factors?

Make one side zero first. If the quadratic factors, a product of two factors is zero when at least one of them is zero.

What if I can isolate a square?

Complete the square to turn the quadratic equation into a squared bracket equal to a constant. This shows which square roots can occur.

Which coefficients enter the formula?

Write the equation with zero on one side. Read the signed coefficients of the square, the first power and the constant.
mistakes: Setting individual factors equal to zero only works when their product is zero.
A negative value on the right of a real square gives no real root.
Keep exact radical form when the question asks for an exact value.

examples.title: Use the zero-product rule
examples.question: Solve \(x^2-1x-20=0\). Give both roots.
examples.solution:
Factorise using two numbers whose product is the constant and whose sum is the middle coefficient.

The equation becomes \((x+4)(x-5)=0\). Set each factor equal to zero.

The answer is \(x=-4\ \text{or}\ x=5\).

examples.title: Solve using a completed square
examples.question: Solve \(x^2-10x-11=0\) by completing the square. Give both roots.
examples.solution:
Complete the square: \((x-5)^2=36\) after moving the constant.

Take both square roots. Then add 5 to each of the two answers.

The answer is \(x=-1\ \text{or}\ x=11\).

examples.title: Use the quadratic formula for exact roots
examples.question: Solve \(x^2+13x-6=0\) using the quadratic formula. Give both roots exactly.
examples.solution:
The coefficients are \(a=1\), \(b=13\) and \(c=-6\), so the discriminant is \(193\).

Substitute the coefficients into the quadratic formula and keep both signs before the square root.

The answer is \(x=\frac{-13\pm\sqrt{193}}{2}\).

lessons.title: A linear and a nonlinear equation together (Extended)
lessons.summary: Substitute from the line, solve the quadratic and recover all the matching ordered pairs.
lessons.objective: Substitute from the line, solve the quadratic and recover all the matching ordered pairs.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Find every x value, then use the fixed y for both pairs.

Find the matching y for each x separately.

After solving the quadratic, substitute in the line and check the product.
lessons.method:
How can a horizontal line meet a curve?

The line fixes y at one value. Substitute that value into the curve to find the x coordinates where they meet.

What changes when the line slopes?

The line still gives an expression for y. Set that expression equal to the curve's expression and solve for x.

How can I handle a product of two unknowns?

Use the line to replace one factor of the product. The remaining equation uses just one letter.
mistakes: List the complete pairs even when they share the same y value.
Putting the same y value into both pairs can lose one of the intersections.
Check each pair against both conditions, rather than listing all x and y values separately.

examples.title: Find all matching pairs
examples.question: Solve \(y=6\) and \(y=x^2-1x-14\) together. Give all ordered pairs \((x,y)\).
examples.solution:
Replace y in the curve equation by the value \(6\) from the line.

Solve \(x^2-1x-20=0\), for x values \(-4\) and \(5\). Substitute each x into the line to find its matching y.

The answer is \((-4,6),\ (5,6)\).

examples.title: Find all matching pairs
examples.question: Solve \(y=6x+8\) and \(y=x^2+5x-22\) together. Give all ordered pairs \((x,y)\).
examples.solution:
Set the right-hand sides equal since both give y. Move the linear expression to the other side.

Solve \(x^2-1x-30=0\), for x values \(-5\) and \(6\). Substitute each x into the line to find its matching y.

The answer is \((-5,-22),\ (6,44)\).

examples.title: Find all matching pairs
examples.question: Solve \(x+y=1\) and \(xy=-42\) together. Give all ordered pairs \((x,y)\).
examples.solution:
Replace y in the product equation by \(1-x\). Expand and rearrange to a quadratic.

Solve \(x^2-1x-42=0\), for x values \(-6\) and \(7\). Substitute each x into the line to find its matching y.

The answer is \((-6,7),\ (7,-6)\).

lessons.title: Changing the subject with powers and repeated terms (Extended)
lessons.summary: Collect repeated subject terms or undo roots and powers with the stated sign condition.
lessons.objective: Collect repeated subject terms or undo roots and powers with the stated sign condition.
lessons.before: Choose an operation that keeps the original relationship true.
lessons.ideas:
Write the letter once as a factor outside a bracket.

Check the sign condition before squaring. Keep the rest of the radicand grouped.

State the sign condition. Without one a real squared equation can have two signs.
lessons.method:
What if the new subject appears twice?

Bring both terms containing the new subject to the same side. Factor out that letter before dividing.

How do I undo a square root?

Isolate the root, then square both sides. A principal square root has a non-negative value.

Which square root is allowed after rearranging?

Once a squared subject is isolated, read the sign restriction. In a length formula the appropriate root is non-negative.
mistakes: If dividing by an expression, that expression must be non-zero.
Do not square only part of a fraction.
If the problem gives a physical length, check that the proposed value fits its domain.

examples.title: Collect repeated appearances of the subject
examples.question: Make x the subject of \(s=kx-5x\), where \(k\ne 5\).
examples.solution:
Factor out the common x to obtain \(s=(k-5)x\).

Divide both sides by \(k-5\), which is non-zero.

The answer is \(x=\frac{s}{k-5}\).

examples.title: Undo a square root in a formula
examples.question: Given \(r=5\sqrt{x+6}\) with \(r\ge0\), make x the subject.
examples.solution:
Divide by \(5\) and square both sides to undo the square root.

Subtract \(6\) to leave x by itself.

The answer is \(x=\frac{r^2}{25}-6\).

examples.title: Rearrange a squared variable with a sign condition
examples.question: Given \(q=7x^2+7\) and \(x\ge0\), rearrange the formula to give x in terms of q.
examples.solution:
Subtract \(7\) and divide by \(7\) to isolate the square.

The intermediate expression gives x squared. Then take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\).

Take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\). \(x=\sqrt{\frac{q-7}{7}}\).

questions.hint_html: List the two excluded values before solving.
questions.solution_html:
Exclude \(x=\pm1\). Multiply every term by \((x-1)(x+1)\).

Expand and rearrange to \(x^2+4x-165=0\). Factorise as \((x-11)(x+15)=0\); neither candidate was excluded.

The answer is \(x=-15\ \text{or}\ x=11\).

1. Given \(q=9x^2+7\) and \(x\ge0\), rearrange the formula to give x in terms of q.

    Show your working.

    [2]

  2. Make x the subject of \(s=kx-153x\), where \(k\ne 153\).

    Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract \(7\) and divide by \(9\) to isolate the square.

The intermediate expression gives x squared. Then take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\).

Take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\). \(x=\sqrt{\frac{q-7}{9}}\).

(b)

Factor out the common x to obtain \(s=(k-153)x\).

Divide both sides by \(k-153\), which is non-zero.

The answer is \(x=\frac{s}{k-153}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Isolate the square before taking the root.

(b)

Keep the terms involving x together, then factor out x.
